strengths: The paper addresses a major challenge in generative molecular dynamics—transferability and data efficiency—by systematically evaluating whether auxiliary pretrained representations (pLMs, structural foundation models, and LLM metadata) improve implicit transfer operators.

Remarkable compute and data efficiency: PLaTITO-Big achieves superior or competitive equilibrium distribution sampling metrics (MAE, RMSE, Coverage) on out-of-distribution fast-folding proteins compared to state-of-the-art Boltzmann emulators (BioEmu) while requiring ~8x fewer GPU hours and ~4x less aggregate MD simulation data.

The evaluation covers a broad spectrum of biophysical observables, including equilibrium free-energy landscapes via TICA projections, long-timescale transition kinetics (MFPTs), temperature-dependent non-Arrhenius rates, and cryptic binding pocket transitions.

Transparent and rigorous empirical analysis, including negative results: the authors openly show that LLM-derived metadata annotations fail to provide a useful conditioning signal and slightly degrade performance.
The paper and appendices are exceptionally well-structured and clear, providing full algorithmic descriptions, training/sampling hyperparameters, and inference throughput benchmarks.
weaknesses: The model operates strictly on a coarse-grained C-alpha backbone representation. While this facilitates scaling and comparison on global conformational landscapes, side-chain packing is critical for real-world downstream biophysical applications such as cryptic pocket druggability and ligand binding.

Transition timescales are quantitatively underestimated by a factor of 2 to 5 compared to reference MD (e.g., folding MFPT for A3D of 5.5 µs vs 27 µs in MD). Although partially rationalized by the variational principle, this limits the direct quantitative utility of the kinetic rates.

The architecture relies on non-equivariant transformers with only center-of-mass subtraction (Algorithms 1 & 2). The manuscript does not clearly specify how rotational invariance or equivariance is handled or if the model relies purely on coordinate frame canonicalization/augmentation during training.

Sampling of cryptic binding pockets remains largely diffuse: as shown in Figures 6 and 12, PLaTITO-Big tends to sample broad, flat ensembles rather than resolving distinct, sharply separated metastable apo and holo free-energy wells.

strengths: High data and compute efficiency: PLaTITO demonstrates that conditioning coarse-grained Implicit Transfer Operators on pretrained protein language model (pLM) representations matches or outperforms Boltzmann Emulators (such as BioEmu) while requiring roughly an order of magnitude less MD training data (56 ms vs. 216 ms) and training compute (~1,100 vs. 9,216 GPU hours).

Thorough and systematic ablation study: The manuscript cleanly decouples the contributions of sequence embeddings (ESM Cambrian), structural priors (Proteina), and metadata annotations (LLM-derived), transparently documenting both the significant benefits of pLM representations and the failure of LLM prompt conditioning.

Broad dynamical and kinetic validation: Beyond evaluating static equilibrium free-energy landscapes across the fast-folding benchmark suite, the authors investigate kinetic observables, demonstrating continuous 120-microsecond trajectories with repeated folding/unfolding events and recovery of non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent kinetics.

Comprehensive empirical reporting: The appendix provides extensive qualitative and quantitative evidence, including full TICA projections across all test proteins, detailed training/sampling hyperparameters, inference throughput measurements on modern GPU hardware, and concrete failure analysis on cryptic binding pockets.
weaknesses: Coarse-grained resolution limits biophysical granularity: The framework operates strictly on C-alpha backbone representations, which omits side-chain packing, allosteric rotamer shifts, and steric interactions that are critical for drug discovery and high-resolution pocket characterization.

Quantitative discrepancy in kinetic rates: As noted in Section 5.3, the mean first passage times (MFPT) predicted by PLaTITO-Big systematically underestimate reference MD timescales by a factor of 2 to 5 (e.g., folding MFPT of 5.5 µs vs. 27 µs for A3D). While qualitatively consistent, this gap restricts quantitative kinetic utility.

Diffuse free-energy landscapes on cryptic pocket benchmarks: In the cryptic binding pocket evaluations (Figure 6 and Figure 12), PLaTITO-Big produces relatively flat, unimodal distributions without clearly resolved metastable basins, failing to separate apo and holo states in two out of four targets.

Lack of theoretical physical preservation: Unlike exact Boltzmann generators or physics-constrained operators, the iterative rollout of the learned flow-matching velocity field offers no theoretical guarantees of detailed balance, invariant measure preservation, or Chapman-Kolmogorov semigroup consistency across consecutive steps.

strengths: Compelling demonstration of data efficiency: The paper convincingly demonstrates that conditioning implicit transfer operators (ITO) on pretrained protein language model (pLM) embeddings substantially improves out-of-distribution generalization while using significantly less training data (56 ms vs. 216 ms + AFDB) and compute (~1,100 GPU hours vs. 9,216 GPU hours) compared to Boltzmann Emulators like BioEmu.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The authors conduct a systematic ablation across different auxiliary modalities (pLM sequence embeddings, Proteina structural embeddings, and LLM-derived quality filtering), transparently reporting both successes (pLM, structure) and failures (LLM metadata).

Evaluation beyond static equilibrium ensembles: Unlike many generative protein dynamics papers that only evaluate marginal conformer distributions, this work assesses dynamical and kinetic properties, demonstrating continuous 120-microsecond rollouts with reversible folding/unfolding events and non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent rate trends.

Clear writing, reproducible algorithms, and detailed appendices: The core flow matching formulation, network design, training hyperparameters, and sampling procedures are documented with precision in Algorithms 1-3 and Tables 2-4.
weaknesses: Unequal comparison between coarse-grained and all-atom models: PLaTITO operates strictly on coarse-grained C-alpha coordinates ($x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{3L}$), whereas BioEmu models full-atom representations and was evaluated on atomistic features. Comparing compute hours (1,100 vs. 9,216) and claiming superiority over BioEmu in Table 1 is partially an apples-to-oranges comparison, as coarse-graining reduces the spatial degrees of freedom by an order of magnitude.

Poor energetic barrier definition and shallow metastable basins: As illustrated in the cryptic pocket benchmarks (Figures 6 and 12) and several fast-folders (Figures 7-10, e.g., Protein G, Homeodomain, lambda-repressor), the model often samples diffuse, broad distributions rather than distinct, sharp metastable basins with proper energetic separation.

Systematic underestimation of dynamical timescales: The mean first passage times (MFPT) for folding and unfolding are consistently underestimated by a factor of 2 to 5 compared to ground-truth MD (e.g., folding MFPT of 5.5 microseconds vs. 27 microseconds in A3D). While the authors cite the variational principle as an explanation, this remains a significant practical limitation for quantitative kinetic surrogate modeling.

Limited novelty in core machine learning methodology: The flow matching ITO formulation and the non-equivariant Proteina-based transformer architecture are direct adaptations of existing work (Schreiner et al., Geffner et al.). The primary methodological novelty consists of concatenating frozen external embeddings to the conditioning representations.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem in generative molecular dynamics: improving the data efficiency and generalization of transferable implicit transfer operators across unseen protein systems.

Strong empirical performance: PLaTITO-19M achieves state-of-the-art results on standard equilibrium sampling benchmarks (fast-folding proteins), outperforming strong baselines like BioEmu, ConfDiff, and Str2Str in free energy MAE and RMSE while requiring ~8x less compute and ~4x less training data.

Comprehensive and insightful ablations: the authors systematically explore multiple auxiliary conditioning modalities (sequence pLM embeddings, structure embeddings, and LLM-derived quality annotations), different pLM scales/families (ESMC 300M to 6B, ESM2), and model parameter scaling (1M to 100M).

Physical validation extends beyond static distributions: the paper evaluates dynamical observables, demonstrating repeated folding/unfolding events in multi-microsecond rollouts, non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent kinetics, and exploration of cryptic binding pocket states.
Clear, structured writing with thorough algorithmic details, hyperparameter specifications, and reproducible descriptions in the appendix.
weaknesses: The model operates solely on coarse-grained C-alpha representations, omitting side-chain conformations and explicit solvent interactions, which restricts its immediate utility for fine-grained biochemical tasks such as ligand binding specificity.

While the model reproduces qualitative kinetic phenomena (such as non-Arrhenius temperature trends), the absolute timescales (mean first-passage times) are systematically underestimated compared to MD references (e.g., folding/unfolding MFPTs ~3-5x faster), meaning generated trajectories lack calibrated physical time.

Conditioning on LLM-derived annotations degraded performance compared to PLaTITO; while honestly reported, the paper offers limited analysis into why the reasoning signals failed to guide the dynamics or whether alternative conditioning mechanisms could resolve this.
Evaluation on cryptic binding pockets reveals that PLaTITO-19M tends to sample broad ensembles without forming well-defined metastable basins for the apo/holo states in several test cases.

strengths: Compelling data and compute efficiency: PLaTITO-19M achieves superior free-energy landscape estimation on fast-folding proteins compared to state-of-the-art models like BioEmu (MAE 0.824 vs 1.110; RMSE 1.099 vs 1.389), while requiring nearly an order of magnitude less MD training data (56 ms vs 216 ms) and training compute (~1,100 vs ~9,216 GPU hours).

Novel and insightful integration of pLM representations into dynamic surrogates: The paper convincingly demonstrates that conditioning implicit transfer operators on pretrained protein language model (pLM) embeddings significantly boosts out-of-distribution transferability and generalization across unseen protein systems.

Comprehensive physical and dynamical validation: The evaluation extends well beyond stationary equilibrium distributions to include dynamic observables, such as continuous long-timescale folding/unfolding trajectories (120 µs), mean first passage times (MFPTs), recovery of non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent kinetics, and transitions in cryptic binding pockets.

Extensive and systematic ablations: The authors provide detailed ablation studies dissecting model capacity (1M to 100M parameters), pLM size/family (ESMC 300M, 600M, 6B, and ESM2), auxiliary conditioning sources (structure embeddings and LLM annotations), and alternative baselines (ConfDiff, Str2Str, Emu).

Honest discussion of failure modes and theoretical limitations: The manuscript transparently notes the limitations of the operator (e.g., systematic underestimation of timescales in accordance with variational principles, lack of detailed balance/semi-group consistency, and difficulties in resolving deep metastable basins in some cryptic pockets).
weaknesses: Coarse-grained representation: The model operates exclusively on $C_\alpha$ coordinates. While coarse-graining reduces computational complexity, it omits side-chain packing and all-atom interactions, which are critical for many downstream biophysical applications like precise ligand binding or side-chain-driven allostery.

Limited effectiveness of auxiliary modalities beyond pLMs: Structure embeddings provide only marginal quantitative improvements over pLM representations alone, and LLM-derived metadata actually hurts performance (MAE degrades from 0.949 to 1.066), suggesting that the multimodal conditioning framework's utility is currently driven almost solely by the sequence embeddings.

Lack of exact physical symmetries: The underlying architecture relies on a non-equivariant transformer with center-of-gravity subtraction rather than an SE(3)-equivariant formulation, which may necessitate learning rotational invariance from data diversity rather than guaranteeing it by construction.

Timescale compression in kinetic observables: Although the model captures qualitative folding/unfolding transitions and non-Arrhenius trends, predicted MFPTs are systematically faster than explicit-solvent MD benchmarks by a factor of 2–5, indicating that the surrogate accelerates transition kinetics relative to physical reality.

strengths: Compelling demonstration of data and compute efficiency: PLaTITO achieves lower MAE and RMSE on the fast-folding protein equilibrium benchmark than large-scale emulators like BioEmu while requiring ~8x less compute (1,100 vs. 9,216 GPU hours) and significantly less training data.

Comprehensive empirical investigation and ablations: The authors systematically evaluate several conditioning modalities (sequence embeddings from multiple pLM families and scales, structural embeddings from Proteina, and LLM-derived domain annotations) alongside scaling sweeps from 1M to 100M parameters.

Evaluation beyond equilibrium distributions: In addition to free-energy surface projections in TICA coordinates, the study rigorously examines kinetic properties, demonstrating continuous folding/unfolding transitions, non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent rate behaviors, and sampling of cryptic binding pocket states.

Well-structured presentation and reproducibility details: The manuscript provides explicit training and sampling pseudocode (Algorithms 1–3), full hyperparameter tables, inference throughput benchmarks across different protein lengths (Table 11), and per-protein free-energy landscapes in the appendix.
weaknesses: Coarse-grained representation limit: Modeling only $C_\alpha$ backbone atoms limits utility for practical downstream tasks such as ligand binding specificity, side-chain packings, and atomistic drug design compared to all-atom surrogate frameworks.

Kinetic timescales and lack of dynamical guarantees: The model systematically underestimates transition timescales (e.g., A3D folding mean first-passage time of 5.5 µs vs. 27 µs reference MD), and standard transfer operator validations like Chapman-Kolmogorov semigroup consistency tests or detailed balance verification are absent.

Mixed performance on cryptic binding pockets: In two of the four cryptic pocket test systems (Q29495 and Q58L87), PLaTITO-19M fails to recover the apo state, and the resulting free-energy landscapes show broad, diffuse distributions without clearly defined metastable free-energy basins.

Negative result with LLM annotations: Adding LLM-derived suitability and confidence features consistently degrades equilibrium sampling metrics (Table 1, MAE increasing from 0.938/0.949 to 1.066), suggesting that the proposed heuristic metadata integration injects noise rather than beneficial physical prior knowledge.
